<reason>B built the cleaner path to the motion as written. Its three-pillar case (contestation, accuracy, enforcement precondition) survived intact, and its rebuttals did real damage: the toothless-vs-corrupting contradiction charge forced A onto the defensive, the "false choice" turn neutralized the one-bite argument, and B's Q1 extracted a critical concession — nothing in the motion blocks substantive rules too. A's counter depended on a speculative political-sequencing claim and on arguing for a different regime (cause standards) that B showed presupposes disclosure anyway. A was more original and rhetorically striking (the compliance-shield inversion, "document describing her powerlessness"), and landed genuine hits on the fraud-exemption gap and filing-as-standard-of-care. But B4.3's flip — inspectors, unions, and advocates can act on information even when individual workers can't — went effectively unanswered, and B's closing crystallized the decision rule: documented power is reachable, silence manufactures no liability. A's clipped Rebuttal 1 was a small additional execution cost. Clear but competitive win for PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 opening salvo ([B2.1]): the charge that CON's pillars contradict — disclosure either changes nothing or corrupts everything — plus [B2.4]'s reversal of "one bite at the apple" into "transparency is the floor substance stands on." A's asymmetric-power reply was clever, but B4.3's counter (regulators, unions, advocates can act; the worker never stood alone) reclaimed the exchange and A never answered it.</best_rebuttal>
